Journal of the House of Representatives of the State of New-Hampshire, June 1804 session, pp. 46-47 (HathiTrust uiug.30112108098069): "Yeas 81-Nays; 73. So it paffed to be enacted." (long-s OCR). DECISIVE: New Hampshire was the 13th of 17 states, completing the 12th Amendment. Margin 5.2 points - the narrowest decisive-state vote in this dataset. Gov. John Taylor Gilman then VETOED the ratifying act on 1804-06-20 and the House failed to repass it ("Yeas 76-Nays; 68. So it does not become a Law, there not being two thirds of the members in favour of it."); the orthodox view is that Article V vests the power in the legislature so the veto is irrelevant.

Omaha Daily Bee, 1919-01-17, p.2, quoting the Nebraska Secretary of State's telegram verbatim: "yeas, 98; nays, 0." DECISIVE: the House concurrence in the Senate joint resolution at 10:25 a.m. completed Nebraska's ratification and made it the 36th state. Headline same page: "NEBRASKA PUTS DRY AMENDMENT IN FORCE BY VOTE / Thirty-Sixth State to Ratify". Nebraska was bicameral in 1919 (the unicameral began 1937).
Omaha Daily Bee, 1919-01-17, p.2, quoting the Nebraska Secretary of State's telegram: "oil the 14th instant: Yeas, 31; Nays, / 1." ("oil" is OCR of "on"; the nay count wraps to the next line).

PRECURSOR VOTE, not the operative one. Omaha Daily Bee, 1919-01-16, p.1: "96 for and none against". On 1919-01-15 the House adopted its OWN ratification resolution 96-0 (three members absent); the same article states this "does not complete ratification for Nebraska". Final action was the 98-0 on the Senate resolution the next morning.

Journal of the Senate of the State of Ohio, 59th session = v.66, 1870, p. 44, Friday January 14 1870, on Senate Joint Resolution No. 4: "The question then being on the adoption of said resolution, The yeas and nays were ordered, and resulted - yeas 19, nays 18, as follows: Those who voted in the affirmative were - Messrs. Bartram, Bell, Corey, Dunbar, Everett, Gatch, Goepper, Howard, Jones, McKinney, Odlin, Potts, Root, Stimson, Streator, Wade, Welsh, Woodworth and Yeatman - 19. Those who voted in the negative were - Messrs. Amos, Boesel, Burt, Campbell, Cowan, Daugherty, Emmitt, Hibbs, Holden, Hubbell, Hunt, Jamison, Jenner, Leeds, Lord, Prophet, Winner and Woodbridge - 18. So the resolution was adopted. The preamble was agreed to." The printed name lists count to exactly 19 and 18; 19+18 = the whole 37-member Senate. This is the vote Mathews (1909) meant by "a margin of one vote in the Senate," citing Ohio Senate Journal 1870 p. 44. Immediately before it the same page records a motion to postpone to the second Monday of January next, lost 18-19. Ohio's date of record, 1870-01-27, is not the day either chamber voted: it is the day the enrolled resolution was signed. House Journal 1870 p. 110 carries the enrollment report on S. J. R. No. 4 and p. 111 records "The Speaker then, in the presence of the House, signed said Senate joint resolution No. 4," both under the date Thursday, January 27, 1870. Source: HathiTrust full view, item coo.31924012209890, scan seq 50; page text saved to data/raw/ratmargins/ohio-1870-journals-hathitrust-pages.txt. Ohio counted 26th, not decisive (Iowa was 28th).

PRIMARY ROLL CALL. Journal of the House of Representatives of the State of Ohio, 59th session = v.66, 1870, p. 89: "Mr. Dodds asked to be excused from voting on S. J. R. No. 4. He was excused. The question being on the adoption of S. J. R. No. 4, Ratifying the proposed 15th Amendment to the Constitution of the United States, The yeas and nays were ordered, and resulted - yeas 57, nays 55 ... So said joint resolution was adopted." The printed name lists count to exactly 57 and 55. The roll call closed the sitting that convened Thursday January 20 1870 and is printed under the running head "Friday, January 21, 1870"; pp. 87-88 carry "Thursday, January 20, 1870," and the House message reporting concurrence to the Senate is dated January 21, 1870 (Senate Journal p. 72). Mathews (1909) cited House Journal 1870 p. 88 for "a margin of ... two in the House"; p. 88 in fact carries the two preliminary roll calls (previous question ordered 57-55; the Dodds substitute submitting the amendment to a popular vote rejected 55-57) and the adoption roll call itself begins on p. 89. NO VOTE COUNT APPEARS ANYWHERE IN THE INSTRUMENT. House of Delegates acted 1791-12-05; Senate concurred 1791-12-15. Virginia was the 11th of 14 states, completing Amendments 1-10. Four independent contemporaneous accounts (Evening Star 1913-02-03 p.2; Omaha Daily Bee, Charlotte Daily Observer and Asheville Citizen, all 1913-02-04) report the Delaware action with a clock time and no vote count; the ~25-minute Senate-then-House sequence indicates suspension of the rules. The 1913 Delaware House and Senate Journals are held by the Delaware Public Archives and are not online.

Mr. Gartrell of Cobb called for a division of the question, and upon his motion the vote was taken upon the first resolution, when the same was adopted. PRIMARY ROLL CALL. DECISIVE STATE: Iowa was the 28th of 37 and completed the Fifteenth Amendment. Journal of the Senate of the Thirteenth General Assembly of the State of Iowa, 1870, p. 77, sitting of January 26, 1870. The Senate had refused to concur in the House joint resolution and a conference committee reported a substitute text; "On motion, report was taken up and considered, and report of Committee adopted. On motion of Senator Bennett, the rule was suspended, and the joint resolution read a third time. On the question, 'Shall the joint resolution pass?' The yeas were - Senators Allen, Atkins, Beardsley, Bennett, Bill, Bulis, Campbell, Cathcart, Chapin, Claussen, Couch, Dixon, Donnan, Dysart, Griffith, Grimes, Hamilton, Havens, Hawley, Hurley, Ireland, Keller, Larrabee, Long, Lowry, McKean, McNutt, Mitchell, Moore, Murray, Newell, Patterson, Pierce, Rice, Smyth, Traverse, Tuttle, Vale, Vermillion, West, Wolf, and Wright - 42. The nays were - Senators Casady, Dunham, Fairall, Fellows, Knoll, McCulloch, and Mulkern - 7. Absent or not voting - Senator Clark - 1. So the joint resolution passed and the title was agreed to." 42+7+1 = the 50-member Senate. At the next sitting, January 27, "Senators Bill and McNutt asked leave to record their vote in the affirmative, on the proposed 15th article to the Constitution of the United States. Leave was granted. Senator Fellows asked leave to record his vote on same subject in the negative. Leave was granted." - the printed tally already includes all three. Iowa's date of record, 1870-02-03, is the date of the governor's approval and certificate, not of either chamber's vote. Iowa is absent from Mathews (1909).
